History:
• 40-year-old female presents with 3-week history of decreased hearing on the left side and constant numbness over the left periauricular region and jawline.  
• Associated symptoms: intermittent ringing (tinnitus) in the left ear and occasional dizziness during ringing episodes.  
• Denies limb weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria, visual changes, ear discharge, otalgia, fever, or pruritus.  
• No known precipitating trauma or infection.  
• Occupational impact: reduced training as a jockey due to dizziness.  

Past Medical History:
• Nasal polyps – uses intranasal spray as needed (name/dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Remote history of labyrinthitis (resolved).  
• Occasional dyspepsia – uses Rennie (antacid; dose/route/frequency not documented).  
Allergies: Latex.  
Medications: Intranasal spray for polyps PRN; Rennie PRN; no other regular medications reported.  
Family History: Brother with neurofibromatosis.  
Social: Works as a jockey; lives with partner; no pets; no other social risk factors discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Video consultation only; no hands-on examination performed.  
• Patient appears alert and conversational; no obvious facial asymmetry documented.  
• Further neurological and otoscopic examination deferred to in-person visit.

Impression:
• Suspected left-sided Bell’s palsy causing hypoesthesia and hearing changes; other neurologic pathology to be ruled out.

Management Plan:
• Urgent same-day face-to-face clinic appointment arranged for full neurological exam and ear inspection.  
• Admin team to contact patient; patient instructed to phone support line in 5 minutes to schedule convenient slot in Central London clinic today.  
• Reassured that presentation is unlikely to be life-threatening but requires confirmation.  
• Further treatment (e.g., corticosteroids, antivirals) to be considered once diagnosis confirmed.

Patient Summary:
Ms. Mary Richards has developed left ear hypoacusis, facial numbness, tinnitus, and occasional dizziness over 3 weeks. Presentation most consistent with Bell’s palsy, but in-person neuro-otologic evaluation is required today to confirm and guide therapy.

Key Takeaways:
1. Attend in-person clinic appointment today for full examination.  
2. Call the support team within 5 minutes to book the slot.  
3. Condition is unlikely fatal; timely assessment will clarify diagnosis and start treatment promptly.

Next Steps:
• Complete neurological and otoscopic examination today.  
• If Bell’s palsy confirmed, initiate oral corticosteroids ± antivirals per guideline and provide eye-care advice.  
• Consider audiometry and MRI/CT if exam suggests alternative pathology.  
• Follow-up visit after initial treatment or sooner if symptoms worsen.
